title: Welcome to a World of Fish Helmets and Floating Tokens: The Weird, Wonderful Art of Trevor Winkfield
summary: Have you ever dreamed of a place where nothing quite makes sense, but everything feels colorful and exciting? That’s the world of Trevor Winkfield, a British-born artist who has been painting mysterious, playful scenes for decades. A new show in New York City, called “The Mermaid’s Revenge,” displays eight of his paintings from the 1990s and early 2000s. Winkfield’s art is like a puzzle you don’t need to solve. He uses bright, flat colors — think playroom reds, blues, and yellows — and fills his canvases with strange details. In one painting, “The Student,” a young man wears a helmet with a fish on top and what looks like a lock over one eye. He holds a long pot under a lightbulb that drops little tokens marked with snowflakes. Those same tokens float in the sky outside the window! His body is pieced together like a collage, with hands and feet painted in different colors, including soft green and orange. Why? Winkfield doesn’t explain. He wants us to enjoy the mystery. Winkfield moved to New York in 1969 and became friends with poets and writers. He even translated a book by Raymond Roussel, a famously odd French writer who used word games to create his stories. Some people think Winkfield’s paintings are like Roussel’s tales, but Winkfield says there’s no secret code. He just loves making images that are both cheerful and a little bit spooky — what one writer calls “cheerfully sinister.” The figures in his paintings are often alone, doing curious tasks: a navigator, an astrologer, even a self-portrait with a palette and tiny paint dabs. Winkfield paints on a table, and these works are bigger than his usual ones — some as wide as a grown-up’s arm span! The show runs through July 31 at Tibor de Nagy gallery. If you like art that makes your brain tingle with questions, this is your ticket to a one-of-a-kind adventure.
why_it_matters: Art that doesn’t give you a clear answer teaches you that it’s okay not to know everything and that curiosity and imagination are just as important as facts.

background_read: Trevor Winkfield was born in England in 1943 and moved to New York in 1969, where he became friends with poets and artists.
His art is often described as surreal, meaning it mixes everyday objects in dreamlike and surprising ways, like something from a colorful dream.
The Tibor de Nagy gallery has a long history of showing artists who break the rules and try new things.

WHERE: Tibor de Nagy gallery in New York City
WHY: To invite viewers into a world where nothing needs to make perfect sense but everything feels exciting

perspectives.description: People who enjoy puzzles and riddles find Winkfield’s paintings endlessly fascinating because they can always discover new details.
Some might say the art is too strange or confusing, preferring pictures that clearly show people or places they recognize.
Experts see his work as part of a long tradition of artists who playfully challenge the way we see reality, like famous surrealist painters.
